new_statements.quote: Для тиндинского языка характерно нечетко выраженное динамическое подвижное ударение. Место ударения не фиксировано и не зависит от фонетического состава слова. Оно связано либо с семантикой, либо с количеством слогов в слове [1–5]. [...] На первом слоге ударение может быть разной интенсивности (сильное – слабое). [...] На втором и последующих слогах ударение обычно сильное [...] Ударение на заимствованных словах показывает, что исторически в тиндинском языке оно было преимущественно на первом слоге [...] [p.107] В подавляющем большинстве двухсложных исконных субстантивов ударение падает на первый слог [...] [p.108] В большинстве глаголов ударение падает на первый слог.
new_statements.translation: Tindi is characterised by a weakly expressed dynamic mobile stress. The place of stress is not fixed and does not depend on the phonetic make-up of the word. It is connected either with semantics or with the number of syllables in the word. [...] On the first syllable stress may be of different intensity (strong - weak). [...] On the second and following syllables stress is usually strong [...] Stress on loanwords shows that historically in Tindi it was predominantly on the first syllable [...] In the overwhelming majority of disyllabic native nouns stress falls on the first syllable [...] In most verbs stress falls on the first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Magomedova, Patimat T. 2014. Ob udarenii v tindinskom jazyke [On stress in Tindi]. Vestnik Dagestanskogo nauchnogo centra 52: 106-109.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position: stress is weak, dynamic and mobile, lexically/morphologically determined and contrastive (minimal pairs by place, e.g. rázi 'handful' vs razí 'in agreement', and by strong vs weak initial stress, e.g. q'áru 'boot-top' vs q'àru 'time'). Default tendency is initial: most disyllabic native nouns and most verbs are stressed on the first syllable; some nouns on the second; native adjectives stress the suffix -áb/-úb; certain inflectional affixes (some plural and genitive suffixes, imperative, negative, participle/converb, optative and conditional endings, ordinal -lIáb) attract stress, while prohibitive, masdar and past endings do not; weak initial stress may shift rightward under suffixation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described; instead a strong vs weak intensity contrast of (initial) primary stress is described (strong marked with acute, weak with grave).
new_statements.exceptions: Avar/oriental loans often shift stress (ilqí > ʕérqi 'herd'); Russian loans less adapted; compounds usually stress the first member, a minority the second; adverbial adjectives in -ssa never stress the suffix; locative vs additive case forms distinguished by stress (hiní 'inside' vs híni 'inward'). Magomedbekova 1999: 285 concurs: 'Ударение слабое, динамическое, подвижное. Его место в ряде случаев соотносится с морфологическим классом данного слова. Ударение может быть смыслоразличительным (ъагьа́ 'наверх' – ъа́гьа 'обломок').'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms and inflected word forms; author notes the system is 'нечетко выраженное' (weakly expressed) and that for noun inflection she could not establish a regularity; Borise 2020 mentions an attempted tonal reanalysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Tindi proper (speech of the auls Tindi and Echeda); Magomedbekova 1999 sec. 2.0.0 states explicitly that the description is based on the Tindi-proper dialect, as opposed to the Aknada-Angida dialect. Language-level glottocode tind1238; no sub-dialect glottocode asserted. Note Glottolog lists Magomedbekova 1999 at pp. 258-265, but in the held printing (signed to press 16.11.2000) the chapter is at pp. 283-290.

new_statements.quote: Starostin (1978: 88), Kibrik et al. (1978: 44) and Nikolaev (2000: 154) also report on collective fieldwork on Tindi performed in 1974, during which Aknada Tindi was tentatively described as possessing three distinct tones: ‘rising’, ‘falling’ and ‘levelled’, which apply to a word as a whole. [...] Stress was analyzed as targeting syllables with ‘rising’ tone. An instrumental investigation, however, revealed that the supposedly tonal distinctions are attributable to the interplay of vowel length and stress. [...] Pitch distinctions that also accompany these vowel length contrasts turned out to be weak and unstable (Nikolaev 2000: 155). See also Borise-stress (this volume), section 6.2 for a non-tonal analysis of Tindi.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Magomedova 2014 statement (weakly expressed, dynamic, mobile stress, place not fixed, minimal pairs). It adds the prosodic-type detail that the pitch/tone contrasts once claimed for Tindi are not phonemic tone but vowel length interacting with stress, i.e. the language is to be catalogued as a stress language, not a tonal one. It says nothing about where stress falls, so it neither confirms nor challenges the 'lexical (unpredictable)' placement reading. (For the record, the companion Borise-stress chapter, lingbuzz/004203, already held at, sec. 6.2, printed p. 18, summarises Magomedova 2012/2014: 'Stress tends to be initial in both nouns and verbs', strong vs w…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The chapter gives no placement rule for Tindi word stress. It reports that the 1974 Starostin/Kibrik/Kodzasov/Nikolaev fieldwork tentatively analysed Aknada Tindi as having three word-level tones (rising, falling, levelled), with stress landing on rising-tone syllables, and that instrumental work (Nikolaev 2000: 155) then reduced these 'tones' to vowel length plus stress, with pitch weak and unstable; sec. 5 (p. 25) repeats that Tindi was 'first analyzed as tonal' but 'later turned out to be based on a feature other than pitch, such as vowel length'. So the work's usable content is: Tindi is a stress language, not a tone language; for stress placement it defers to the companion chapter (Borise-stress, sec. 6.2).
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect difference reported from the 1974 fieldwork: Aknada Tindi with three 'tones' vs other dialects merging 'rising' and 'levelled' against 'falling'; on the final syllable of mono- and disyllables, 'rising'/'levelled' correspond to a long vowel and 'falling' to a short vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: The tonal claims discussed by Borise concern the Aknada dialect of Tindi specifically (three 'tones'), with 'other dialects of Tindi' said to merge rising and levelled; Magomedova 2014, the catalog's source, describes Tindi without a dialect restriction.

readall_conflicts: No live conflict with the catalog. The only disagreement Borise 004204 records is historical: the 1974 collective fieldwork (Starostin 1978: 88; Kibrik et al. 1978: 44; Nikolaev 2000: 154) analysed Aknada Tindi as having three word-level tones with stress on rising-tone syllables, whereas the later instrumental investigation (Nikolaev 2000: 155) and the descriptive tradition behind the catalog entry (Magomedbekova 1999, Magomedova 2014: weak, dynamic, mobile stress with minimal pairs) treat Tindi as a stress language whose apparent pitch contrasts reduce to vowel length plus stress; Borise sides with the non-tonal analysis. The catalog's existing reading (lexical, unpredictable) stands; the companion Borise-stress sec. 6.2 adds only a tendency toward initial stress with morphologically conditioned final stress, which is a refinement rather than a contradiction.
